title: Chapter 69 – Feng's Leg
html:
[Azure Cloud Sect – Lin Feng]

The Stillness Chambers cost five points a night, and Feng has paid for eleven of them in the last two months.

They are cells, really. A row of low stone cubes behind the Hall of Elders' Rest, each the size of a grave, each with a single slab of pale jade for a floor and a door of black iron that seals from the inside. The air within is thicker than anywhere else in the Outer Court. It tastes faintly of rain. A servant at the gate takes the points on a slate, and does not look up, and a boy goes in, and shuts the door, and sits.

He sits. He is on the slab with his legs folded and his hands on his knees, in the dark, with a single dim lantern at his shoulder, and he is not breathing.

One, he counts.

It is the fourth try this month. It is the eleventh since the winter. Every night, for five points, he sits in this box and tries to do the one thing a Qi Refining ninth-stage cultivator is supposed to do: gather the Qi of all nine layers and drive it, in a single sustained push, into the dantian, until the dantian breaks and what comes out of the break is something new. A Foundation. A second rank.

He has the Qi. He has had the Qi for four months. It sits in him like a lake behind a dam, full to the lip, a thick slow weight of green and red and brown, wood and fire and earth, a triple root that has never once failed him. He can feel the push waiting. He can feel the dam.

Two.

He gathers it. He draws the lake together into a single point, below the navel, and begins, patiently, as a man leans on a stuck door, to lean.

Three.

The dam gives a little. It gives with a long, slow, grinding sound, like a millstone starting to turn. A warmth spreads upward along the spine. It is the beginning of a thing, and for a moment, in the dark and the stone and the smell of rain, he lets himself think of it as something that will happen.

Four.

The leg lights up.

It is always the same. It begins in the left calf, a hand's breadth below the knee, with a cold prick like a splinter, and then it is not a prick but a ring, a thin red band of fire running round the bone. It does not hurt at first. It is only there, a fact, an alarm bell in the dark. Then the lake in his dantian lurches toward it, like water to a drain, and the whole careful structure of the push comes apart, and the Qi pours down his left leg and out into the ground in a long hot scream.

He bites through his lip.

He does not cry out. He has learned that much. He sits on the slab with his teeth locked and his eyes screwed shut and his left hand clamped round his own shin, and waits for the fire to burn itself out. It takes a long time. When he opens his eyes the lantern has guttered, and the slab under him is wet.

Four breaths, he thinks. Four, again.

He is breathing like a runner. He does not move for some time.

It is not the failure that he minds. It is the arithmetic. Five points a night. Eleven nights. Fifty-five points, gone, in a place where a boy at his rank earns thirty a month if he is lucky, and every one of them has bought him exactly four breaths of progress and a bitten lip.

And even if the push worked. Even if the dam broke, and the Qi poured through, and something new rose out of the break.

A second rank without a pill, he thinks, is a coin flip with a knife.

He knows the numbers. Every Outer disciple does. A Foundation Establishment attempt, by Qi alone, succeeds one time in four. The failures are not gentle. A Level 2 pill, a true breakthrough pill of the second rank, raises it to nearly three in four, and the Sect sells them to the Inner and the Core and the True, at six hundred points apiece, and does not sell them to anyone else.

Six hundred. He does the sum again, as he has done it every night. Thirty points a month. Less meals. Less chambers. He will have six hundred when he is thirty-two.

He opens the iron door. The night air is cold and clean. He goes out limping, and his left foot drags on the gravel, and he does not look back at the cell.

* * *

His brother finds him at dawn on the Hundred Stairs.

He has not slept. He never does, after the chambers. He sits on the fortieth tread of the lower flight with his bad leg stretched out in front of him and a rice cake going stale in his hand, and the whole of the mountain stretched beneath him, red roofs and gray terraces and the white scar of the Cloud Road winding away into the plain. The sky is pale. The stair lanterns are still lit, small, steady, golden, a long thread of fire curling up the slope.

"You are early," says Jian.

He has come up the stair without a sound. He is smaller than Feng remembers, thinner, with the gold ring round his eyes that has not faded since the siege and a streak of green on the knee of his robe from the terraces. He has a hoe over his shoulder. He looks, Feng thinks, like a gardener who has wandered into a war.

"I am always early." Feng lifts the rice cake. "Do you want half? It is not good."

"I have eaten."

"You have not. Sit."

Jian sits.

They are quiet for a time. It is a thing they have never had to learn, the two of them, a kind of ease that was there from the beginning: Feng talking too much, and Jian saying too little, and both of them understanding, without explaining, that it comes to the same. A thin wind comes up the stair. Somewhere far below, a servant is sweeping.

"You are not going to ask," says Feng.

"About what?"

"What I do in the Stillness Chambers at night. Why my lip is split." He scrubs the back of his hand across it. "Everyone else has."

"I thought you would tell me, if you wanted."

"It is the leg."

"I know."

"It flares at the fourth breath. Every time. I get to the part where it begins to move, and the scar lights up, and..." He makes a short, sharp gesture, like a man snapping a twig. "I have tried eleven times. I have tried standing, and lying, and in cold water. The Healers say it is a meridian block. They say it will clear in a year." A short laugh. "It has been four."

"It is not a block."

Feng looks at him.

"It is a lock," says Jian. He does not raise his voice. He looks at the leg, and not at Feng's face. "A hook. Something that was put in and has been left to wait. The stair read it, in your first year. Cheng Yun said it was almost gone. I do not think it is gone. I think it is only quiet until you push."

It is exactly what Feng has been afraid of, for four years, in the dark.

"What do I do?" he says.

"I do not know yet." Jian rubs his nose. "I am going to find out. But I will not do it blind. Show me the stair."

* * *

They climb.

It is not a hard flight, at first. The Hundred Stairs begin at the foot of the mountain, a wide white ribbon of stone, fifty paces across, rising in shallow steps. There are no rails. The lanterns burn in niches set into the wall. At the bottom, a servant sells paper charms and hot tea. At the tenth tread, a pair of Keepers in gray stand against a pillar, bored, with their hands in their sleeves.

"It is a pressure array," says Feng, as they start up. He is talking too fast. He knows it, and cannot stop. "It reads you as you climb. Every step is a measure. The array leans on you, a little more each time, as if the whole mountain were pressing on your shoulders. You climb until you cannot. Where you stop, that is what you are." He counts on his fingers. "Forty, they say you are a junior. Sixty, you are named. Eighty, and the Elders write your name in a book."

"And a hundred?"

"Nobody has reached a hundred in three hundred years." A shrug. "I reached seventy-three. In my first year. It is the third-highest in the Outer Court." A pause. "It is also where the scar lit up, and I fell down. So it is only a number."

At thirty, the pressure begins.

Jian has the Veil up. Feng can see it, a faint slow flicker round the boy's shoulders, spring to summer to autumn, as if a small wind were moving through a wheat field. It is a good Veil. He would not have known, if he had not been told. But the pressure is a thing the array does to all of them, Veil or no, and by the thirty-third step the boy has begun to sweat, and his steps are shorter.

"You can stop," says Feng.

"I would like to see it."

"It is at forty. Seven more."

"I would like to see it."

They climb the last seven in silence.

The fortieth landing is a broad, flat platform of white stone, set into the mountain like a terrace, with a low parapet on the outer edge and a wall of black rock behind. Two old Keepers sit at a small table by the parapet, playing a game with black and white stones, and do not look up. A single lantern hangs in the center, higher than the others, and burns with a hard cold light that is not gold at all.

And in the rock wall, at the back of the landing, at the height of a man's chest, there is a plate.

It is round. It is the width of a washbasin, made of some dull pale metal that gives back no reflection, set flush with the stone. Round its rim, cut into the rock, a ring of small notches runs in a perfect circle. They are not carved; they are grown, smooth and clean, like the lobes of a leaf. Feng has counted them a hundred times. He counts them again, for no reason.

"Seven," he says. "There are seven. They are all the same size. They are not decoration." He stops, a pace from the wall. "You can feel it, if you stand here long enough. It hums. Not a sound. A feeling in the teeth. Every night, in the third watch, it hums once, low, and then goes still. The Keepers do not look up. They have been told not to."

"Have you touched it?"

"No." It is almost a whisper. "I told you. It is the kind of thing that watches."

Beside him, the boy has gone absolutely still.

It is not the stillness of a child who is frightened. Feng has seen frightened children. It is the stillness of a man who has been handed a thing he has been looking for, and does not trust his hands. He stands at the edge of the landing, ten paces from the plate, with the hoe still on his shoulder and his face quite blank, and his eyes, the gold-ringed eyes, are moving very slowly round the ring of notches. One. Two. Three. His lips move.

Seven, thinks Feng. He is counting them too.

"Jian?"

"It is a strange lock," says Jian, in a voice that is entirely level.

"It is not a lock. Not exactly." Feng looks at the plate. "Last year I asked an old Keeper. He said it was a dock. Then he caught himself, and said, no, a seal. It was the only time anyone has slipped." A small tight breath. "A dock is for something to be put into. A seal is for something to be kept out. I do not know which."

"It would be a dock."

"How do you know?"

"I do not," says Jian. "It is a guess."

It is the first thing the boy has said in two minutes that Feng does not believe.

He does not say so. He stands, a little behind and to the left of his brother, in the cold white lamplight, with the stones clicking softly on the Keepers' table, and thinks, very clearly, the one thought he has never let himself finish. He knows what it is.

And it is not mine to ask.

* * *

The leg gives out on the way down.

It is not the pressure. It is the thirty-fourth step, where the pressure begins to ease, and the body, relieved, forgets to be careful. His foot comes down on a tread that is a hair's breadth too narrow. The scar flares. He feels the red ring tighten round the bone like a wire, and the leg goes out from under him, and he sits down hard on the white stone with a sound that is half a curse and half a groan.

"Feng!"

"It is nothing." It is not nothing. He cannot feel the foot. He grips the knee in both hands and rocks, a little, grinding his teeth. "It is the scar. It does this. It will pass in a moment."

It does not pass.

Jian has dropped to a crouch beside him. He has laid his palm flat on the calf, below the knee, where the ring of fire runs, and is frowning at it with an expression Feng has seen only on Hu, bent over a bad casting. His eyes have gone very far away.

"It is moving," he says.

"What?"

"The hook. It is not a ring. It is a coil. It is turning, slowly, under the skin." He looks up. "How long has it been doing this?"

"Always." Feng's voice is thin. "It is only worse when I push."

"No. It is worse when it is looked at." Jian takes his hand away. His face is gray. "When you push, you look at it. It looks back. That is the trouble. Whatever it is, it does not want to be seen."

It is a thing that watches, thinks Feng, absurdly. Like the plate.

They take him to the Healing Hall in a hired chair.

It is a mean, low building at the edge of the Outer Court, with a smell of camphor and wet linen. A healer sees them in a narrow room: a short, bald, ink-stained man with a tired face and a roll of linen bandages round his wrist. He is perhaps fifty. His name is Song. He listens to the story, without comment, with his thumb pressed against Feng's shin, and when he has finished, he is silent for so long that the sound of rain begins on the roof.

"It is a hook," he says.

"I told him."

"No. You said a block. A block is a swelling of the meridian. This is a hook." He turns the leg a little, gently, to the light. "A blood hook. A thread of an old Qi cut, set in the bone at a vital point. It is a very fine piece of work." A thin, grim pause. "Whoever put it there did so as a child, I would say. Six, seven years ago. A sleeper. A thing set to wake when the host reaches a certain cultivation, so that the one who set it may find him."

"Find him," says Feng.

"Or kill him. Or use him. It depends on the maker."

He says it so calmly that for a moment Feng does not understand.

"Can it be removed?"

"Of course." Song lets go of the leg. "A Level 2 Clear Vein Pill. Two doses, ten days apart, and a day in a cultivation chamber under a Healer's eye. It takes the hook out, root and stem. It will cost you, at the Hall's price..." He glances at the slate on the wall. "Four hundred points."

It is a number. It is a perfectly ordinary one. It is only that it falls, in the quiet of the room, like a stone into a well.

"I have eighty-one," says Feng.

"Then you will need a longer life." The healer's face is not unkind. "Or an Elder who owes you a favor. Or four hundred and nineteen points, which are generally harder to come by." He looks at the boy, and his face softens, by a degree. "I will not pretend. It is the common cost of a bad inheritance. I have seen it a dozen times. The ones who wait too long..."

He does not finish.

He gives Feng a salve for the swelling, and a pill for the pain, and a tight small bow. And then, as they reach the door, he says, almost to himself, in a low voice:

"It is an odd thing."

"What?"

"The cut." Song is looking at the wall. "It is a Court cut. Not Blood Shadow. Blood Shadow make hooks with a hooked blade. This was made with a straight one, the kind we use in the Hall, for opening a vein to read it. It is the pattern the Enforcement Hall's own readers learn in their second year." He shakes his head, slowly. "I should not say that. I am an old man. It is probably a coincidence."

The door closes behind them.

* * *

They eat at the long hall at noon.

Feng does not want to. He has no appetite, and his leg is a hot throb from knee to heel, and the salve smells of old cheese. But the rule is the rule, and a boy who skips two meals is looked at, and he has, in the last three hours, been looked at enough.

He orders for both of them. It is not a decision. He walks to the slate, and takes two wooden bowls, and says to the clerk: "Lin Feng. Eighty-one. Two bowls, with egg."

"Two bowls are two points. With egg, four."

"Four, then."

"Both on your slate?"

"Both on mine."

The clerk looks at him, and at the boy beside him, and at the thin gray slip of bamboo in Jian's hand. She is a stout, weary woman with a bun of gray hair. She marks the slate without a word.

"You do not have to," says Jian, when they are seated. He has not touched the bowl. "I have twenty-nine in debt. I will clear it in a month."

"You will clear it in a month if you are not sick, and do not miss a day, and Overseer Han does not find a leaf out of place." Feng pushes a boiled egg across the table with one finger. "I know. I did my first year. Eat."

"It is your points."

"They are not mine. I cannot spend them on the leg. I cannot spend them on the pill. I cannot buy my way into a Stillness Chamber and make it count." He picks up his spoon and puts it down again. "Eighty-one points will not save me, Jian. They might save you. So eat the egg."

For a moment the boy does not move. Then, slowly, he lifts his bowl.

It is a very small thing, to watch a person eat. Feng has done it for twenty years, across a table in a cold house, in the long lean winters when there was not enough to go round. He has never in his life thought of it as a gift. He thinks of it now. He does not say so.

"I have something to tell you," says Jian, in a low voice.

"Not here."

"Here. It is quiet enough." He looks round. At the far end of the hall, a knot of older boys is laughing over a game of dice. At the nearer table, two servants are quarreling about a bucket. The noise is a thick, warm, forgetful wall. "The Garden has a door. In the paving, by the pool. It is a round plate, broken at the edge. I found it in the autumn."

Feng puts down his spoon.

"It opened for me. Once." The boy's voice is steady. "It opened one stair. A very short one. I went down, and I looked, and I came back." He does not look up. "That is all I will say. That is all I can say. There is a reason. I am sorry."

"One stair," says Feng.

"One."

"And at the bottom?"

"A room. A small one." The boy swallows. "There is nothing in it now."

Now.

Feng hears the word. He puts it away, very carefully, with the others. A plate in a wall. A seven-lobed ring. A stair that opens for a hand.

A dock, he thinks. For something that was put in.

He thinks of the notes in his own hand, written a year ago, in a cold room, by a boy who did not know what he was writing. There is a lock at the fortieth. I have never once wanted to see what is behind it. He had meant it. He had been afraid.

He is not afraid now. It is a strange feeling. It is the feeling of a man who has been standing for a year at the edge of a pool, and has just watched his brother walk into it.

"I will not ask," he says. His voice is very rough. "I want you to know that. Whatever it is. Whatever you took." He picks up his spoon. "I am not going to ask."

"You do not have to..."

"I know I do not have to. That is why I am telling you."

The boy looks at him.

He does not say anything. He puts the egg in his mouth, and chews, and swallows, and looks at the bowl. It is a long moment before Feng realizes that his brother's eyes are wet.

* * *

They part at the foot of the stair, in the evening, with the lamps coming on.

Jian has duty at dusk, a second shift on Terrace Nine, and goes off along the lower path with his hoe over his shoulder, a small gray figure in the gold light. Feng watches him until he is out of sight. Then he turns, and begins, slowly, with a hand on the wall, to climb.

It is the long way round. He takes the lower stair, and not the lift. His leg is bad, and the pain is a steady red pulse, and he is not in a hurry. At the first landing he stops, and sits on the parapet, and takes out of his sleeve the small round tube of bamboo that he has worn at his neck since the summer.

It is Jian's talisman. It is a Mirror Guard, a thing that held a blood-arts cultivator at bay for fifty-eight breaths in a closed room, and it is nearly spent. He turns it in his fingers. He does not open it.

Whoever put that scar on me, he thinks, did it with the Enforcement Hall's own knife.

I was ten.

He had been at home, then, in the long cold house on Green Pine Hill. A man had come in the winter, an examiner of the Sect's Outer Court, kind and soft-spoken, in a gray robe, with a lamp. He had looked at every child in the house. He had laid a hand on each of their heads. When he reached Feng, he had said something, very softly, that Feng had not heard. And in the night, his leg had burned.

He had not remembered it in years. It had come to him on the stair, and in the clinic, like a flavor on the tongue.

A kind man, he thinks. A man with a lamp.

The mountain is darkening. The lanterns on the long stair have begun to glow, one by one, a thread of small gold stars climbing into the dusk. Far above, at the fortieth landing, a single white light burns, hard and cold, like an eye.

He sits on the parapet for a long time, with the cold bamboo in his hand.

It is in this Court, he thinks. It was always in this Court. Whoever put that scar on me is here.

And I have been climbing past him every day.
